title: Pliny's Letters: Ghosts and Apparitions, Letters to Trajan and Calpurnia

guide.summary: Unit 3 covers Pliny's letters on ghosts and apparitions (7.27), his official correspondence with the emperor Trajan, including the famous exchange about Christians (10.96–97), and his affectionate letters to his wife Calpurnia (6.4, 6.7, 7.5), revealing different sides of Pliny's self-presentation.

sections.heading: Ghosts and apparitions (7.27)
sections.body: Writing to Sura, Pliny asks whether ghosts (phantasmata) exist or are just products of fear. He offers examples: Curtius Rufus, in Africa, is met by a woman of superhuman size who foretells his future, which comes true; and the philosopher Athenodorus rents a cheap, notorious house in Athens where a ghost of a thin old man in chains appears at night. Athenodorus calmly keeps writing, then follows the ghost to a spot in the courtyard where it vanishes; when the ground is dug up, bones in chains are found and given proper burial, and the haunting ends. The letter blends curiosity, storytelling, and the Roman concern for proper burial; the sight passage above retells the Athenodorus story in different Latin.

sections.heading: Letters to Trajan (10.96–97)
sections.body: As governor of Bithynia-Pontus, Pliny writes to Trajan for guidance on how to treat people accused of being Christians. He describes his procedure: he asked the accused three times, executed those who persisted (judging their stubbornness deserving of punishment), and released those who denied it, offered incense and wine to the emperor's image and the gods, and cursed Christ. He reports that Christians met before dawn on a fixed day and sang a hymn to Christ as to a god, and that questioning two enslaved women called ministrae revealed only a 'depraved and excessive superstition'. Trajan replies that Christians are not to be sought out, those accused and convicted are to be punished, those who deny and worship the gods are to be pardoned, and anonymous accusations must not be accepted, as they belong to a bad precedent and not to 'our age'. The letters show Roman provincial administration, legal caution, and religious policy.

sections.heading: Letters to Calpurnia
sections.body: Pliny's letters to his young wife Calpurnia express love and longing during separations: he worries about her health while she recovers in Campania, says he holds her letters as a substitute for her presence, and describes how at night his feet lead him to her empty room. These letters, intimate yet carefully composed for publication, show the Roman ideal of affectionate marriage and Pliny's self-image as a devoted husband. Comparing them with the official letters to Trajan highlights shifts in tone, register, and purpose.

keyTakeaways: Athenodorus and the chained ghost; proper burial.
Letters vary in tone by recipient and purpose.
commonMistakes: Saying Trajan ordered Christians to be hunted down (he said not to seek them out).
Reading the Calpurnia letters as private rather than published.
examTips: Compare register across letters (official vs intimate).
Use the phrase conquirendi non sunt accurately.
Connect the ghost story to Roman burial customs.

practice.prompt:
Read the summary of Pliny, Letter 10.96, and Trajan's reply, Letter 10.97, and answer both parts. Support your claims with references to the letters (cite Latin you have studied where possible).

**Summary:** Pliny describes how he questioned people accused of being Christians, punished those who persisted, and released those who denied it and worshipped the gods and the emperor's image; he asks Trajan whether his procedure is correct. Trajan approves, adding that Christians should not be sought out and that anonymous accusations should not be accepted.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: How does Pliny present himself in Letter 10.96?

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: What policy does Trajan establish in Letter 10.97, and what does it suggest about Roman government?

rubric.description: Clear claim about how Pliny presents himself (cautious, legalistic, deferential).
Specific evidence from 10.96 (asking three times, seeking guidance, testing procedure).
Clear claim about Trajan's policy (restraint, legality, fairness).
Specific evidence from 10.97 (conquirendi non sunt; rejection of anonymous accusations).

practice.sampleResponse:
A. Pliny presents himself as a careful and loyal administrator who wants to act lawfully. He explains his procedure in detail, asking the accused three times whether they were Christians and punishing only those who persisted, and he asks Trajan directly whether he has acted correctly. By seeking the emperor's guidance instead of acting on his own authority, he shows deference and caution.

B. Trajan's reply establishes a policy of restraint. He says that Christians are not to be sought out (conquirendi non sunt), though those accused and convicted must be punished, and that anyone who denies it and worships the gods should be pardoned. He also forbids anonymous accusations, saying they set a bad example and are unworthy of the present age. The emperor thus balances order with legal fairness.
